spots.name: Florence Cathedral (the Duomo)
spots.label: Duomo

text.description:
Florence Cathedral, formally Santa Maria del Fiore, is the great marble church whose great dome rises above the city. Work began in 1296 and the dome, engineered by Filippo Brunelleschi, was finished in 1436. It is still the largest masonry dome ever built, and it went up without a temporary wooden frame to support it. The walls are faced in bands of white, green and pink marble, and the ornate west front is a 19th-century addition, completed in 1887. The cathedral stands with the Baptistery and Giotto's Campanile in Piazza del Duomo, part of the UNESCO-listed historic centre.

Up close the building is too big to fit into one frame. From the left side of the terrace you get a wide, raised view of the dome rising above the terracotta rooftops, with the river and its bridges in the same shot. The cathedral is the focus, but the city around it makes the picture. It is a free viewpoint and easy to reach, but it fills up fast at sunset, so arrive early and claim a spot at the railing. If you want a higher, clearer view, San Miniato al Monte is a steep walk uphill from the piazzale.
text.directions_text: For the cathedral itself, take tram T1 or T2 to Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella and walk south-east, about 11 minutes on foot. Alternatively, take tram T2 to San Marco Università and walk south, about 9 minutes on foot. For the viewpoint, Piazzale Michelangelo lies south-east of the cathedral across the Arno, about 21 minutes on foot in a straight line, with a climb at the end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: Piazzale Michelangelo is an open public square, but the cathedral is a working place of worship and entry to it and the dome may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in Piazza del Duomo in the historic centre of Florence. The viewpoint, Piazzale Michelangelo, is on the hill across the Arno to the south-east.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole scene, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the dome closer. The cathedral is over a kilometre away, so it looks small at 1x. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a big sweep of sky and rooftops, because the dome will become very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the wall to keep the phone steady. Panorama mode works well for the full sweep of the skyline if you pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset. Arrive early at sunset, as the terrace fills quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazzale Michelangelo (left side of the terrace). A wide, elevated panorama of the cathedral dome rising above the terracotta rooftops, with the Arno and the bridges in the same frame. At the left side of the terrace. The cathedral lies to the north-west, and from here you can see the dome above the rooftops, with the Arno and its bridges in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome on one of the upper intersections, with the river along the lower third. Keep the horizon level. Zoom in a little (2x-3x) so the dome stands out from the rooftops, but leave the river in view. If the terrace is crowded, wait for a gap or hold the phone slightly above the heads in front of you. San Miniato al Monte, on the higher hill, is a good alternative viewpoint with fewer obstructions.

spots.name: Uffizi
spots.label: Uffizi

text.description:
The Uffizi is Florence's great Renaissance art museum, but for a phone photographer the real picture is outside, in the long courtyard in front of it. Two tall, matching wings run down either side of a narrow open square towards the River Arno. At the far end a Doric screen frames the view without blocking it, and the Ponte Vecchio shows in the distance between the arms of the colonnade.

Giorgio Vasari began the building in 1560 for Cosimo I de' Medici, as offices for the city's administration (uffizi means 'offices'). It was finished in 1581. Vasari stressed the perspective by giving both facades continuous roof cornices and unbroken cornices between the storeys, and by adding three long steps along the fronts. That is why the lines pull your eye so strongly towards the river. The niches between the columns were filled with sculptures of famous artists in the 19th century, which give you good detail shots.

The best viewpoint is at the north end of the courtyard, so walk to that end and face south towards the Arno. Keep yourself in the middle so both wings look symmetrical. The square gets very busy, so early morning before the museum opens, or after dark, gives you the clearest view. If you want a wider view of the river, with the Uffizi sitting alongside the Ponte Vecchio and the Palazzo Vecchio tower, Ponte alle Grazie is a good second choice.
text.directions_text: The nearest tram stop is Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 and tram T2). The Uffizi lies to the south-east of it, about 17 minutes on foot. San Marco Università (tram T2) is also close, with the Uffizi to the south, again about 17 minutes on foot. Florence has no metro, so most people walk the last part. Once you are in the historic centre, head for the Piazza della Signoria and the Uffizi courtyard is right beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The courtyard is an open public square, but going inside the Uffizi needs a museum ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Uffizi is in the Historic Centre of Florence, right next to the Piazza della Signoria, with its courtyard opening onto the River Arno.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so both wings of the colonnade fit in and their lines run towards the river. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched version. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pull the Ponte Vecchio closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far end of the courtyard to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning before the museum opens, or at night, when the courtyard is quietest. At other times it is very busy with visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazzale degli Uffizi (north end of the courtyard, shooting south toward the Arno). The symmetrical colonnaded courtyard of the Uffizi, converging toward the Arno, with the Ponte Vecchio visible in the distance between the arms of the colonnade. Walk to the north end of the courtyard on Piazzale degli Uffizi and face south towards the Arno. From there the colonnaded courtyard runs away from you towards the river, with the Ponte Vecchio visible in the distance between the arms of the colonnade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the centre line on the middle of the courtyard so the two sides mirror each other. Hold the phone level, because tilting it makes the walls lean. For a different shot, take a close-up of the statues in the niches between the columns. If you want a wider view of the river, with the Uffizi, the Ponte Vecchio and the Palazzo Vecchio tower together, go to Ponte alle Grazie.

spots.name: Ponte Vecchio
spots.label: Ponte Vecchio

text.description:
The Ponte Vecchio is Florence's old stone bridge over the Arno, lined with small jewellers' shops and crossed on foot by a steady stream of visitors. The current bridge dates from about 1339-1345 and has three shallow arches, the middle one spanning 30 metres. It was the only Florence bridge spared in the Second World War. Above the shops runs the Vasari Corridor, built in 1565 to link the Palazzo Vecchio with the Palazzo Pitti.

Most people photograph the bridge from the crowded Ponte Santa Trinita. The riverside walk also gives close reflections in the water. The bridge's back shops, added in the seventeenth century, are visible from upriver, so look for those jutting out over the water.

Keep the arches and the water in one frame and let the bridge sit across the picture. If you want the classic profile with the hills behind, Ponte Santa Trinita is the alternative. For the wider view with the Duomo and Palazzo Vecchio, try Piazzale Michelangelo and use your phone's zoom.
text.directions_text: From the tram stop Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 and tram T2), the bridge lies to the south, about 1 km away. Head south towards the river and the bridge, then follow the north bank of the Arno to Lungarno degli Archibusieri, at the far end of the street near the Ponte Vecchio. From the Duomo, walk south-west towards the river. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The riverside street and the bridge are open to pedestrians, but the Vasari Corridor and the Uffizi terrace need a ticket and advance booking, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Florence, where the Arno runs between the Uffizi side on the north bank and the Oltrarno on the south bank.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the three arches. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close to the river wall and want to include the reflections. Telephoto (2x-5x) is useful for the shopfronts and the covered passage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge's stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. If the sun is low, try a Live Photo, which lets you pick the best frame of the moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is quieter. Sunset spots in Florence get crowded, so allow extra time if you go then.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lungarno degli Archibusieri (north bank, at the far end of the street near the Ponte Vecchio). The bridge's three arches seen from river level, with the covered passage on its side leading toward the Uffizi. On Lungarno degli Archibusieri, on the north bank at the far end of the street near the Ponte Vecchio. Face south-west and you see the bridge's three arches from river level, with the covered passage on its side leading toward the Uffizi.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arches along the lower third, with their reflections in the water. Keep the horizon straight so the arches don't look tilted. For the bridge in profile with the hills behind, walk to Ponte Santa Trinita instead.
